'''Leo Koenigsberger'''<!--Despite being german, the family name is not written with an ö (see gravestone, his son Johann or german wiki)--> (15 October 1837 – 15 December 1921) was a German mathematician and [[history of science|historian of science]]. He is best known for his three-volume biography<ref>{{Cite book|last=Königsberger|first=Leo|url=http://histmath-heidelberg.de/htmg/HHelmholtz.htm|title=Hermann von Helmholtz|publisher=|year=|isbn=|location=|pages=}}</ref> of [[Hermann von Helmholtz]], which remains the standard reference on the subject. 

== Biography ==
Leo Koenigsberger was born in 1837 in Posen (now [[Poznań]], [[Poland]]) to the wealthy merchant Jakob Löb (1800–1882) and Henriette Kantorowicz (1810–1895) and had eleven siblings.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Knobloch |first=Eberhard |author-link=Eberhard Knobloch|url=https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/gnd116293802.html |title=Neue Deutsche Biographie 12 |date=1980 |pages=355-356 |chapter=Koenigsberger, Leo}}</ref> He studied at the [[University of Berlin]] with [[Karl Weierstrass]], where he taught mathematics and physics (1860–64). He taught at the [[University of Greifswald]] (assistant professor, 1864–66; professor, 1866–69), the [[University of Heidelberg]] (1869–75), the [[Technische Universität Dresden]] (1875–77), and the [[University of Vienna]] (1877–84) before returning to [[Heidelberg]] in 1884, where remained until his retirement in 1914.{{sfn|Rines|1920}}

Whilst at Heidelberg, he was elected to honorary membership of the [[Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society]] on 17 April 1895.<ref> Memoirs and proceedings of the Manchester Literary & Philosophical Society v43 1998-1899</ref>

In 1904 he was a Plenary Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in Heidelberg.<ref>{{cite book|chapter=''Gedächtnisrede auf C. G. J. Jacobi'' by L. Königsberger|pages=57–85|title=Verhandlungen des dritten Mathematiker-Kongresses in Heidelberg von 8. bis 13. August 1904|location=Leipzig|publisher=B. G. Teubner|year=1905|chapter-url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=miun.aag4063.0004.001;view=1up;seq=71}}</ref> In 1919 he published his autobiography, ''Mein Leben'' ('My Life'). The biography of Helmholtz was published in 1902 and 1903. He also wrote a biography of [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi|C. G. J. Jacobi]].{{sfn|Rines|1920}}

Koenigsberger's own research was primarily on [[elliptic function]]s and [[differential equation]]s. He worked closely with [[Lazarus Fuchs]], a childhood friend.{{sfn|Rines|1920}}

In 1873, he married in Heidelberg Sophie Beral-Kappel, daughter of the merchant Iwanowitsch Beral of Kharkov and Anna Grigoriewna Tschaikowski. They had a son and a daughter, [[Johann Koenigsberger]] (1874), professor of physics in Freiburg, and Ani Koenigsberger (1876).<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Koenigsberger Leo |url=https://www.leo-bw.de/web/guest/detail/-/Detail/details/PERSON/kgl_biographien/116293802/biografie |access-date=2025-11-03 |website=Landesarchiv Baden-Württemberg}}</ref>
